summary: A visual tool that lets astronauts track their own health and get a smart diagnosis when no hospital is within reach. It simulates 30 biomarkers across an Earth, deep-space and Mars mission, detects anomalies, classifies them into 8 conditions, forecasts problems 3 days ahead, and tells the crew what to do next.
details:
In our project, We aim to include the following :

  • Our solution is a visual tool to track astronauts health and smart diagnosis system
  • Help astronauts and guide them with procedures and treatments
  • Gather data from biomarkers sensors both HF and LF and other crew members notes and remarks
  • Questions to directly answer : - Which measurements can be performed in space? - Why is an exam needed? - How do spaceflight hazards affect these health indicators? - When might a result warrant attention from the crew or from flight surgeons on the ground? - What actions can be taken to prevent a critical health condition?
  • Present Metrics and Diagnosis clearly
  • Schedule astronauts to take certain measures and exercises as part of their mission
  • Color coding to instantly notice anomalies
  • Dynamic charts that shows trends and measurements of vital biomarkers
  • A visual tool that lets astronauts track their own health and get a smart diagnosis, with no hospital within reach
  • It collects data from biomarker sensors and crewmate remarks, explains what the numbers mean, and tells the crew what to do next
  • Journey covered: Earth surface, then deep space, then the Mars surface
  • On Mars a message takes 3 to 22 minutes each way, and there is no quick evacuation. The crew must be able to assess their own health.
  • Spaceflight hazards change the body quietly, often with no symptoms until they are serious. Regular exams catch the change early, while a countermeasure can still work.
  • NASA's Human Research Program groups the risks into five hazards. We organise our 30 biomarkers around them:

1. Space radiation

  • Damages blood cells, raises inflammation and long-term disease risk
  • Indicators: absorbed radiation dose, lymphocyte count, IL-6, TNF-alpha

2. Isolation and confinement

  • Stress, disrupted sleep, mood changes and tension inside a small team
  • Indicators: resting heart rate, heart-rate variability (HRV), sleep duration, sleep efficiency, plus crewmate remarks (planned)

3. Distance from Earth

  • Delayed communication, limited resupply and food variety, and no fast medical help, so nutrition and self-monitoring matter
  • Indicators: calories, protein, vitamin D, omega-3, zinc, magnesium, blood glucose, hydration, body weight

4. Gravity fields

  • Weightlessness shifts fluids toward the head and unloads bones and muscles. Mars gravity is only about 38% of Earth's, and landing adds another adjustment.
  • Indicators: retinal thickness, refraction shift, visual acuity, jugular vein flow, vein stasis, micro-clots, calf circumference, bone loss rate, T-score, bone turnover ratio, urinary calcium

5. Hostile and closed environments

  • A sealed habitat shares air, water and surfaces, so microbes spread more easily
  • Indicators: microbial count (CFU rate), body temperature
  • 30 biomarkers, grouped into 8 conditions: heart and sleep, nutrition, eyes, bone and kidney, inflammation, neck veins and fluid shift, radiation, and metabolism and hydration
  • High-frequency (HF) sensors: heart rate, HRV and radiation dose, sampled every few minutes
  • Low-frequency (LF) measures: daily or periodic values such as weight, blood and urine tests, ultrasound and eye scans, chosen because they fit a spacecraft medical kit
  • Crew remarks (planned feature): every crew member can record remarks about his crewmates, for example "more irritable than usual" or "keeps skipping meals"

Why peer remarks matter

  • People often under-report fatigue, low mood or stress, so a self-assessment of "I'm fine" can be falsely healthy
  • Sensors cannot see morale or behavioural-health problems
  • Remarks from crewmates close that gap. One remark is only a note, but repeated, independent remarks about the same person raise a flag, and they are weighed together with the sensor data for the isolation and confinement hazard.
  • Built on published science: normal ranges and thresholds come from academic and research sources used by NASA's Human Research Program. Where a published limit was missing, the team documented an assumption for expert review.
  • Hypothetical missions: with those thresholds we generate simulated Earth, transit and Mars trips for different astronauts, with realistic slow changes (bone loss, fluid shift, radiation dose)
  • Scripted events: we add events to those trips, for example an inflammation episode with fever, a tachycardia episode, a stress collapse after landing and a glucose rise, with different timing for each astronaut
  • A trained model: all of that data trains a smart model that detects anomalies and trends and classifies them into 8 conditions
  • Honest testing: the model is trained on some missions, tuned on another and tested on a mission it has never seen. It is tuned against the known events to catch real problems and keep false alarms low.

How it decides

  • Detect: each day every biomarker is compared with its normal range, the astronaut's own baseline, and its usual day-to-day change
  • Classify: related biomarkers are grouped into a condition score
  • Predict: the model estimates the chance a condition becomes abnormal within 3 days and names the main driver
  • Body map: each body part is clickable and coloured by its condition, with a plain-language explanation
  • Colour coding: green is normal, yellow is a forecast warning, orange is urgent, red is critical (critical parts pulse)
  • Dynamic charts: live lines with a green normal band and red limit lines, updating in real time
  • Daily report: a timeline of every mission day, a table of symptoms with trend arrows, and the days left before a value leaves the normal range
  • Guidance per condition: every diagnosis comes with a plain-language explanation and suggested actions, for example resistive exercise and hydration for bone loss, or a repeat ultrasound for vein risk
  • When to escalate:
    • Critical value: contact the flight surgeon at once
    • Persistent urgent value or a sudden spike: re-measure, then report
    • Forecast warning: start the countermeasure now
  • Act before it is critical: the 3-day forecast gives the crew time to prevent a critical condition, not just react to it
  • Next: a mission-routine scheduler for measurements and exercises (see the roadmap on slide 7)

Results on simulated missions

  • 5 of 5 scripted events caught, with 0 false alerts on a test mission
  • Illness forecast reaches AUC of about 0.92 on missions the model never saw, with days of warning before a condition turns abnormal
  • Honest scope: the data is simulated, so this shows the pipeline works. It has not been medically validated.

Built today

  • Detection, 8-condition diagnosis and 3-day forecast
  • Clickable body map, live charts, daily report and colour coding
  • Suggested actions and escalation levels per condition

Roadmap (next steps)

  • Mission routine scheduler: prompts and checklists for measurements and exercises at the right time
  • Engagement system: points and streaks that encourage the crew to keep up their health tasks
  • Crew remarks: the peer-observation input described on slide 3, with review by the flight surgeon
  • Guided measurements: step-by-step instructions for each measurement and why it matters
  • Delay-tolerant sync: reports queue and sync when the link to Earth allows
  • Live data: connect real sensor feeds in place of the simulated missions
  • Expert review: have medical specialists validate thresholds and advice
